title: Web Crawler
problem: Design a polite, scalable web crawler that ingests billions of URLs, respects robots.txt, and avoids both URL-level and content-level duplicates.
summary: A breadth-first crawler (BFS, not DFS — DFS depth is unbounded on the web) fronted by a prioritized URL Frontier that enforces politeness, priority, and freshness. HTML Downloader fetches through a DNS Resolver; the Content Parser validates + normalizes HTML; a 'Content Seen?' check dedupes near-identical bytes via a hash DB; the URL Extractor pulls outbound links; a URL Filter drops blocklisted/disallowed schemes and robots-disallowed paths; a 'URL Seen?' check (Bloom filter + URL Storage) prevents adding duplicates back to the frontier. The dominant design choices are (1) a politeness-aware priority queue per host with front-queue priority bands and back-queue per-host serialization, and (2) a Bloom filter in front of the URL-seen DB so the fast path is a ~200ns RAM check. The main tradeoffs are Bloom false positives (rarely re-crawl), content-hash dedupe missing near-duplicates (A/B-tested pages), and BFS needing politeness discipline to avoid DoS-ing popular hosts. Sized for ~1B pages crawled/month at roughly 400 pages/sec sustained.

functional: Crawl seed URLs and follow outbound links in BFS order
Respect robots.txt directives and Crawl-Delay per host
Enforce politeness: at most one in-flight connection per host and a minimum gap between fetches
Deduplicate URLs globally so the same page is not re-enqueued
Detect near-duplicate content via hash or shingle fingerprint
Persist fetched HTML to durable storage and emit extracted links for indexing
nonFunctional: Sustained throughput of 400 pages per second, peaking at 1K per second
URL-seen lookup under 1 ms for the 99th percentile request
No single host receives more than two requests per second from the crawler
Frontier survives worker restarts without losing pending URLs
Horizontal scalability: add fetcher workers linearly without rebalancing the frontier shards

assumptions: 1B pages crawled per month (~400 pages/sec average, 1K peak)
Average HTML payload 100-500 KB (median ~120 KB); stored compressed ~40 KB
Politeness: ≤ 1 concurrent connection per host, ≥ 500ms between fetches to same host
URL-seen set grows unbounded; at 1B/mo, 10^10 entries after a year
Content-seen set grows with unique pages ≈ 60% of fetched (40% are duplicates)
estimates: Frontier size at steady state: ~10-100M pending URLs
URL-seen Bloom filter: 10^10 entries * 10 bits/entry ≈ 12 GB RAM, 1% false-positive rate
Bandwidth: 400 pages/s * 200KB ≈ 80 MB/s sustained, 200 MB/s peak
Fetcher pool: 1000 QPS / (1 fetch/host/500ms) → target ~500 distinct hosts in flight → ~500 fetcher goroutines per worker, ~4 worker hosts

seed.name: Seed URLs
seed.summary: Static or periodically refreshed list of high-quality starting URLs — the first input to the crawler. The book emphasizes that choosing good seeds is the difference between quick full-web coverage and a biased, narrow crawl.

sections.heading: Choosing seeds
sections.body:
Two strategies the book calls out:
1. Locality-based — pick popular sites from each country/region; split the web by geography or language so coverage is balanced.
2. Topic-based — partition by content type (shopping, sports, healthcare, news) and seed each partition separately.
Good seeds shorten the BFS depth to any reachable page.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Bootstrap the frontier when the crawler starts cold
- Top up the frontier periodically with directory sites (DMOZ-style), news hubs, sitemaps
- Encode per-seed hints (crawl depth cap, priority boost)

sections.heading: Scale
sections.body: Tiny: a few MB. Stored as a YAML/JSON file in a config repo or an S3 object loaded at startup.

sections.heading: Why it's separate
sections.body: Seeding is coarse and cold; the frontier is hot. Mixing them leads to lost seeds on frontier restart.

bottlenecks.title: Biased seed set causes narrow crawl coverage
bottlenecks.trigger: When seeds are concentrated in one language/region/topic, BFS from those seeds reaches only a subgraph of the web. At 1B pages/month, a biased seed can waste the full 80 MB/s bandwidth budget crawling one neighborhood while missing entire regions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Crawl corpus skews heavily to one TLD/language; downstream index has poor recall for queries outside the seeded domains; content-seen dedup ratio climbs above the expected 40% because BFS loops within a tight cluster.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Apply the book's two-part seeding: locality-based partition (top sites per country/language) plus topic-based partition (shopping, news, healthcare, sports). Periodically augment from DMOZ-style directories, Common Crawl host lists, and published sitemaps; encode per-seed priority boosts so each partition gets frontier share.
bottlenecks.detection: Track crawled-pages histogram by TLD, language (CLD3), and topic classifier; alert when any single dimension exceeds e.g. 40% share, or when new-host discovery rate drops below a baseline (e.g. <10K new hosts/day).

bottlenecks.title: Cold-start frontier starvation on restart
bottlenecks.trigger: If the frontier is wiped (corruption, migration, cold deploy) and only the seed file is available, the crawler must rebuild from a few MB of seeds while the fetcher pool wants ~500 distinct hosts in flight. Warm-up to 400 pages/sec sustained can take hours.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call sees fetcher utilization drop to single-digit %, politeness back-queues mostly empty, throughput far below 400 pages/sec target for an extended window after restart.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep seed list large enough (tens of thousands of diverse hosts, not dozens) so BFS fan-out saturates the fetcher pool within minutes. Persist frontier snapshots to disk (already noted in frontier component) and restore from snapshot first, falling back to seeds only on true cold start. Pre-warm robots.txt and DNS caches for top seed hosts at startup.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on fetcher_hosts_in_flight < 100 for >5 min after process start; dashboard for frontier_size with a floor threshold (e.g. <1M pending URLs = degraded).

bottlenecks.title: Stale seed config drifting from the live web
bottlenecks.trigger: Seeds stored as a static YAML/JSON in a config repo or S3 object loaded at startup. Over months, seeded hosts die (DNS NXDOMAIN, permanent 5xx, domain squatted), new high-value hubs appear (new news sites, new TLDs), and priority hints go stale.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rising fraction of seed fetches returning 4xx/5xx/DNS failure; freshness lag on emerging topics; new-host discovery curve flattens because seeds no longer link to the current web frontier.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Automate seed refresh: a weekly job re-scores seeds by recent fetch success rate and PageRank/traffic signals, drops dead hosts, and pulls new candidates from top outbound links of the last crawl. Version the seed file in git with CI validation (every seed resolves + returns 200 on HEAD).
bottlenecks.detection: Metric seed_fetch_success_rate with alert below 95%; weekly report diffing seed file against prior version; track age of seed config with alert if >90 days since last refresh.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the crawler needs a seed list A web crawler works by following links: it fetches a page, extracts its `<a href>` links, and adds those to the frontier to fetch next. But that process has to *start* somewhere — if the frontier is empty, the fetchers have nothing to do. The seed list is the bootstrap input: a curated set of high-quality starting URLs that gives BFS its root set. For a crawler targeting *billions of URLs* across the whole web, the choice of seeds literally determines which subgraph of the web you can reach, because BFS only discovers pages that are eventually linked from a seed. ## What happens without it If you started with, say, 10 random URLs, the crawler would technically run — but it would explore a narrow neighborhood of the web. The operator would see `new-host discovery rate` flatten quickly, the content-seen dedup ratio climb well above the expected 40% (BFS keeps looping inside a small cluster of linked sites), and the index would have terrible recall for anything outside that cluster. The fetcher pool and frontier are fine; they're just being fed a biased diet. ## The numbers The design targets ~500 distinct hosts in flight to sustain 400 pages/sec under the 500ms-per-host politeness rule. If your seed list only contains a few dozen hosts, BFS fan-out needs many hops before you have 500 live hosts — warm-up to full throughput takes hours. A seed list of tens of thousands of diverse hosts saturates the fetcher pool within minutes of startup. ## The trade-off Seeds are a manual curation burden (weekly refresh jobs, dead-host cleanup) — the designer accepted that operational cost because a biased crawl wastes the entire 80 MB/s bandwidth budget on the wrong part of the web.

frontier.name: URL Frontier (priority queue)
frontier.summary: Politeness-aware, multi-priority queue of URLs waiting to be fetched. Enforces the three properties the book emphasizes: politeness, priority, and freshness.

sections.heading: BFS vs DFS
sections.body: The book picks BFS over DFS. DFS depth is effectively unbounded on the web (you can go arbitrarily deep into one site), and it concentrates load on one host. BFS with per-host politeness spreads load evenly across the web graph.

sections.heading: Two-stage structure (Mercator)
sections.body:
```
Front queues: F1..FN (priority bands, e.g. news=1, blogs=3, tail=5) priorities assigned by PageRank / host traffic / freshness
Back queues: B1..BM (one per politeness host, FIFO within a host)
router: pops from Fi weighted by priority, appends to Bj = hash(host)
worker: picks a B queue whose next-allowed-time <= now, fetches head
```

sections.heading: Politeness
sections.body: A single crawler worker NEVER opens two connections to the same host at once. Each back queue maps to a single host and has a `next_earliest_fetch` timestamp (delay between requests, typically ≥ 500ms). A 'mapping table' (host → back queue id) enforces the 1-queue-per-host invariant.

sections.heading: Priority
sections.body: URLs with higher traffic, PageRank, or freshness demand (news, stock tickers) get higher-priority front queues. Lower-priority URLs only drain when front queues are empty.

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.body: Pages must be recrawled periodically — content changes. Recrawl interval is driven by past change frequency and page importance.

sections.heading: Persistence
sections.body: Per the book: majority of URLs are on disk (cheap, durable), with buffers in memory for enqueue/dequeue speed. Disk buffer flushes periodically. A restart doesn't lose millions of pending URLs.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Spider trap (infinite URL space on one host): per-host quota caps contain it; manual blocklist for known traps.
- Noisy neighbor: one giant site can starve others without priority bands.

gained: Durable log is great for replay after crashes
Horizontal scaling to trillions of URLs
lost: Politeness scheduling is awkward on Kafka's FIFO partitions
No native durability if AOF is off

bottlenecks.title: Politeness-induced host starvation under skewed link graph
bottlenecks.trigger: BFS naturally concentrates links on popular hosts (wikipedia.org, youtube.com, example.com). With the 500ms-per-host politeness cap, a single hot host can only drain 2 URLs/sec while its back queue accumulates millions of pending URLs from fan-in across the frontier. At 400 pages/sec overall and 10-100M pending URLs steady-state, a few mega-hosts can hold 20%+ of the frontier hostage.
bottlenecks.symptom: Back queue depth histogram shows extreme skew — top 10 hosts have queues of 1M+ URLs while the long tail drains in seconds. Fetcher workers idle waiting for cool-downs on the hot hosts; overall throughput drops below 400 pages/sec target even though there's plenty of work.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap per-host back queue depth (e.g. 50K URLs); when full, drop or divert low-priority URLs to a cold-storage overflow bucket. Add per-host quota in the URL Filter (max 100K URLs/host/day already specified) and enforce it pre-enqueue, not post-dequeue. For truly mega-hosts, shard the host across multiple back queues keyed by path prefix so multiple fetcher workers can serve it in parallel (with coordinated politeness via a distributed rate limiter like Redis token bucket).
bottlenecks.detection: Emit p50/p99/max back_queue_depth per host every minute; alert when max/p50 > 1000 (extreme skew) or when any single host's queue exceeds 500K. Also track fetcher_idle_waiting_for_host_cooldown_ratio — alert if >30%.

bottlenecks.title: Disk-backed frontier write amplification at 10-100M pending URLs
bottlenecks.trigger: The design keeps the majority of URLs on disk with in-memory buffers. At 400 pages/sec crawled and ~3x discovered:crawled ratio, the frontier ingests ~1200 URL enqueues/sec and ~400 dequeues/sec. With priority reordering across 5 front queues and per-host back queue routing, each URL may be written/rewritten 2-3x during its lifetime. At 10-100M pending URLs and ~200 bytes/URL that's 2-20 GB of working set with ~500 KB/sec of churn plus periodic compactions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Enqueue latency p99 spikes from 8ms to 100ms+ during compactions; frontier size grows unboundedly because enqueue can't keep up with the 1200/sec discovery rate; fetchers starve on empty back queues while the router thread lags behind moving URLs from front → back.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use RocksDB with separate column families per priority band and per-host back queue prefix (exploits prefix locality). Tune with large memtables (512MB) and level compaction with rate limiter capped at 50 MB/sec to avoid compaction stalls. Keep hot back queue heads (next 1000 URLs per active host) in a Redis sorted set for O(log N) pops; use RocksDB only as cold tail storage. Batch enqueues (100 URLs per write) to amortize WAL fsync.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: frontier_enqueue_latency_p99 (alert >50ms), frontier_router_lag_seconds (front → back movement delay, alert >30s), rocksdb_pending_compaction_bytes (alert >10GB), frontier_size growth rate (alert if > dequeue rate for >10min).

bottlenecks.title: Spider traps and cyclic link farms inflating frontier size
bottlenecks.trigger: Dynamic sites generate infinite URL spaces (calendar pages going to year 9999, faceted search with combinatorial query params, session IDs in path). Even with URL normalization in the extractor, a single trap site can inject 100K+ unique URLs/hour into the frontier. At 10-100M steady-state, two or three active traps can double the frontier.
bottlenecks.symptom: Frontier size grows sharply without corresponding increase in unique content (content-seen dedup ratio climbs above the expected 40%); one host's back queue balloons to millions of entries; new-host discovery rate drops because fetcher cycles are burned on trap URLs; storage bill grows but index quality doesn't.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Per-host URL quota enforced in the URL Filter (design already specifies 100K/host/day — make sure it's wired to frontier enqueue path, not just fetch path). Detect trap patterns: alert when a host produces >10K new URLs/hour with <5% content-seen novelty, auto-add to manual blocklist. Cap path depth at 10 (already specified) and query-string cardinality per host at 1K unique values. Use URL template clustering (replace digit runs with \d+) to recognize parametric explosions.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-host metrics: urls_enqueued_per_hour, content_novelty_ratio (unique hashes / pages fetched). Alert when urls_enqueued_per_hour > 10K AND content_novelty_ratio < 0.1. Daily top-20 report of hosts by frontier share, reviewed by on-call.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the frontier exists for this crawler A web crawler is fundamentally a loop: fetch a page, extract its links, fetch those links, repeat. The URL Frontier is the "to-do list" in the middle of that loop — but it can't be a plain FIFO queue, because this crawler has to be *polite*. The problem statement requires respecting robots.txt and not hammering any single host. If you just dumped discovered URLs into a regular queue, BFS would naturally pile up thousands of links to popular hosts like wikipedia.org (because everyone links to Wikipedia), and your fetchers would fire 500 simultaneous requests at it — which is indistinguishable from a DoS attack. The frontier's real job is **scheduling**: given millions of pending URLs, pick the next one such that no host sees more than one connection at a time and at least 500ms passes between requests to the same host. ## What happens without it If you replaced the frontier with a plain queue, the first victim would be the fetcher pool: workers would either double up on the same host (getting your IP banned) or the politeness logic would move into every fetcher, creating a coordination nightmare. You'd also lose prioritization — a breaking news page would wait behind a million blog URLs discovered earlier. ## The numbers At 400 pages/sec sustained with a 500ms-per-host delay, each host can contribute at most 2 pages/sec, so you need **~200 distinct hosts actively draining at all times** (400 ÷ 2). The frontier's per-host back-queue design is what makes 200 hosts drain in parallel while keeping each one under its politeness cap. ## Trade-off The two-stage front/back queue structure is more complex than a single queue, but without that split you can't independently control *priority* (front queues) and *politeness* (back queues).

fetcher.name: HTML Downloader
fetcher.summary: Bank of worker goroutines/threads that issue HTTP GETs and stream responses. The book calls this the HTML Downloader.

sections.heading: Concurrency model
sections.body: Per worker: ~500 coroutines, each pinned to a politeness host. Non-blocking IO (epoll) means one host can pull a downloader goroutine for the full RTT + download (~100-800ms) without starving others. Distribute workers across multiple servers and geographically close to the target host for lower latency.

sections.heading: robots.txt
sections.body: Before any fetch, the downloader checks a local LRU of robots.txt rulesets (keyed by host). On miss, fetch `/robots.txt` with its own low priority and cache. Robots rules are cached so the crawler doesn't re-download them repeatedly. Respect Crawl-Delay if present.

sections.heading: Performance optimizations
sections.body:
1. Distributed crawl: partition URL frontier across many crawl servers.
2. Cache DNS resolutions locally — DNS is synchronous in most resolvers and can dominate tail latency.
3. Geographic distribution — fetch servers close to target hosts.
4. Short timeout — some servers respond slowly or never; set a max wait and move on.
5. Robustness: consistent hashing for downloader pool, save crawl state for graceful restart, exception handling, data validation.

sections.heading: HTTP hygiene
sections.body:
- Send `User-Agent: MyCrawler/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot)` — identify yourself
- Honor `Retry-After` on 429/503
- Cap page size at e.g. 10 MB to avoid megabyte-of-whitespace attacks
- Timeouts: connect 3s, total 15s

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- 4xx/5xx → drop or retry with backoff depending on status
- TLS errors → log and drop
- Slow-loris server → timeout kicks in
- Server trap / crawler trap → detect via URL pattern and blocklist

lost: JVM footprint; harder to customize at scale
Slower throughput per box than custom Go/Rust
Less efficient than Go/Rust for IO-bound fetching

bottlenecks.title: DNS resolution tail latency dominates fetch time
bottlenecks.trigger: At 400 pages/sec sustained across ~500 distinct hosts in flight, a cold DNS lookup adds 20-200ms before any TCP handshake. If the DNS cache hit ratio drops (new-host discovery burst, TTL expiration storms, cache eviction) even 10% cold lookups at 400/sec = 40 lookups/sec each adding ~100ms, which blocks fetcher goroutines and reduces effective concurrency below the 2000 target.
bottlenecks.symptom: Fetcher p99 latency jumps from ~800ms to 2-3s; fetcher_goroutines_active climbs toward concurrency cap; throughput drops below 400 pages/sec even though network bandwidth is under 80 MB/s; tcpdump shows long gaps before SYN packets.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run unbound/dnsmasq local sidecar with 10M-entry cache and 1h minimum TTL override; pre-resolve hosts asynchronously when URLs enter the frontier (prefetch at enqueue time, not fetch time); use c-ares for non-blocking resolution in-process; fall back across multiple upstream resolvers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9) with per-resolver circuit breakers.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric fetcher_dns_lookup_ms p50/p99 (alert p99 > 50ms), dns_cache_hit_ratio (alert < 90%), fetcher_blocked_on_dns_ratio (alert > 5%).

bottlenecks.title: Slow-host goroutine pile-up exhausting fetcher concurrency
bottlenecks.trigger: Fetcher pool is sized at ~500 coroutines per worker targeting ~500 distinct hosts in flight. A handful of slow hosts responding at the 15s total timeout (or slow-loris attackers dribbling bytes) can each pin a goroutine for the full timeout. At 400 pages/sec target, even 50 stuck hosts (10% of active set) occupying goroutines for 15s each means 750 goroutine-seconds tied up — enough to collapse effective parallelism and drop throughput well below target.
bottlenecks.symptom: fetcher_active_goroutines pegged at concurrency cap; per-host latency histogram shows bimodal distribution (fast p50 ~200ms, long tail at 15s ceiling); throughput drops to 100-200 pages/sec; back queues with fast hosts starve waiting for a worker slot.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tighten total timeout to 10s, connect timeout to 2s, and add a per-byte idle timeout (e.g. 2s between chunks) to kill slow-loris. Use adaptive per-host health scoring — after 3 consecutive timeouts, back off that host for 5 minutes (circuit breaker). Cap page body at 10 MB (already specified) and enforce streaming read deadline. Isolate slow hosts into a separate 'quarantine' fetcher pool so they can't starve the main pool.
bottlenecks.detection: fetcher_goroutines_active / concurrency ratio (alert > 0.85 for >2min), fetcher_timeout_rate per host (alert > 10%), fetcher_p99_total_time (alert > 5s), goroutine dump sampling to spot stuck stacks on read.

bottlenecks.title: IP-level ban from aggregating politeness across shared hosting
bottlenecks.trigger: Politeness is enforced per-host (500ms between requests to example.com), but many hosts share the same IP (shared hosting, CDN pools, same /24). At 400 pages/sec across 500 hosts, if 50 of those hosts resolve to the same CDN IP block, that IP sees 100+ req/sec from our crawler — enough to trigger rate limiters or WAF bans, returning 429/503 en masse or blackholing the crawler's egress IP.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden spike in 429/503 responses clustered by target IP or ASN; fetch success rate drops from 99% to 70-80% for specific CDN-fronted sites (Cloudflare, Fastly); some hosts stop responding entirely (TCP RST or timeout) while DNS still resolves; Retry-After headers appear.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add IP-level (not just host-level) politeness: maintain a secondary rate limiter keyed by resolved IP /24, capped e.g. 10 req/sec per /24. Honor Retry-After strictly and apply exponential backoff per host on 429/503. Distribute fetcher workers across multiple egress IPs (book's 'distributed crawl' point) and rotate if an IP gets banned. Publish a clear User-Agent with contact URL so site owners allowlist instead of banning.
bottlenecks.detection: http_response_status_rate{code=429|503} by target_ip_24 (alert > 5%); fetch_success_rate by ASN with baseline comparison; monitor for TCP RST rate per egress IP; track Retry-After headers received per hour.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the HTML Downloader is here The whole point of a web crawler is to actually *go fetch pages from the internet*. Everything else in this design — the frontier, the parser, the dedup filters — is plumbing around that one action. But at 400 pages/sec sustained with billions of URLs queued up, you can't just call `curl` in a loop. The fetcher is a specialized pool of workers that does three things the rest of the system can't: it opens thousands of concurrent HTTP connections without blocking, it enforces the politeness contract (one connection per host, honor `Retry-After`, identify with a real `User-Agent`), and it isolates the slow, unreliable part of the system (the public internet) from the fast internal pipeline. ## What happens without it If the parser called out to HTTP directly, a single slow-loris server dribbling bytes over 15 seconds would pin a parser thread. Your CPU-bound parsers would sit idle waiting on network IO, throughput would collapse, and the frontier would back up into tens of millions of pending URLs. Worse, without a centralized fetcher enforcing politeness, two workers could hit the same host simultaneously — and your IP gets banned from major sites. ## The numbers The design targets ~500 distinct hosts in flight to hit 400 pages/sec under the 500ms-per-host rule (400 ÷ 2 pages/host/sec = 200 hosts minimum, 500 for headroom). Each fetch takes 100–800ms, so you need ~500 concurrent coroutines per worker — something a dedicated async IO pool handles but a naive thread-per-request model cannot. ## Trade-off Splitting fetch from parse adds a queue hop and serialization cost, but it lets you scale network-bound and CPU-bound work independently.

dns.name: DNS Resolver + Cache
dns.summary: Local DNS cache (unbound) sitting in front of public resolvers to keep lookups off the hot path.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: A cold DNS lookup adds 20-200ms to the first fetch of each host. At 400 hosts/sec a global DNS cache hit ratio of 90%+ turns that into a non-issue.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.body: Unbound or dnsmasq with a large cache (e.g. 10M entries, 1h TTL override on short-TTL records). Fallback to Google (8.8.8.8) or Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) on miss.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Upstream resolver rate-limits → distribute across several, add per-resolver circuit breakers.
- Stale cache on IP changes → respect TTL; crawler can re-resolve on connection refused.

gained: No sidecar; same process as fetcher
lost: Cache is per-process → lower hit ratio across a fleet

bottlenecks.title: Cache miss storm from new-host discovery bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: BFS expansion regularly discovers new hosts (crawler targets ~500 distinct hosts in flight and new-host discovery of 10K+/day is normal). When a popular seed or hub page fans out to hundreds of previously-unseen hosts, the local unbound cache misses in a burst, forwarding all misses to upstream resolvers (8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1) within seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: DNS lookup p99 spikes from <1ms (cache-hit) to 100-300ms; fetcher goroutines pile up blocked on resolution; upstream resolver occasionally returns SERVFAIL or rate-limit REFUSED; fetcher throughput drops below 400 pages/sec despite idle bandwidth and CPU.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-resolve hostnames at URL-frontier enqueue time (asynchronously, off the hot path) so by the time the fetcher pops the URL the A record is warm. Run unbound with prefetch: yes and prefetch-key: yes, set cache-min-ttl: 3600 to override short TTLs, and configure 3+ upstream forwarders with round-robin + per-resolver circuit breakers.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on dns_cache_hit_ratio < 90% (5-min window), unbound num.query.tcp + num.query.udp rate vs. cache.hits ratio, and upstream resolver p99 latency > 50ms. Dashboard unbound's cachemiss metric against new-host-discovery rate.

bottlenecks.title: Upstream resolver rate-limiting / blackhole under sustained miss load
bottlenecks.trigger: At 400 pages/sec with even a 5% cache miss rate that's 20 lookups/sec hitting upstream — sustained over hours, public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) apply per-source rate limits or EDNS Client Subnet throttling. During cold-start or after a cache flush the miss rate can momentarily hit 100% (400+ qps upstream).
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden cliff in fetch success rate; DNS returns NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL for hosts that clearly exist; retries make it worse; connect-refused spikes in fetcher; fetcher_blocked_on_dns_ratio climbs above 20%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Fan out across multiple upstream resolvers (Google, Cloudflare, Quad9, OpenDNS, plus your ISP's resolver) with weighted round-robin in unbound's forward-zone. Add per-upstream circuit breakers (mark a resolver down for 30s after 5 consecutive failures). For very high-volume crawlers, run a recursive resolver locally (unbound in recursive mode, not forwarding) to bypass upstream limits entirely — at the cost of more root/TLD traffic.
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-upstream error rate (SERVFAIL, timeout, REFUSED) with alert > 1%; monitor unbound's num.answer.rcode.SERVFAIL counter; alert if any single upstream contributes > 50% of errors (indicates that resolver is throttling us).

bottlenecks.title: Stale cache entries pointing at dead or rotated IPs
bottlenecks.trigger: Design overrides short TTLs up to 1 hour to improve hit ratio, but many CDN-fronted hosts (Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS ELB) publish 30-60s TTLs precisely because IPs rotate. Over a 1-hour override window, cached IPs for dynamic-IP hosts go stale, and the fetcher connects to IPs that no longer serve the host (or serve a different tenant).
bottlenecks.symptom: Rising TCP connect failures (RST or timeout) clustered on specific hosts; TLS SNI mismatches or cert errors when connecting; fetch success rate drops for CDN-hosted sites while DNS lookups appear successful (fast cache hits returning dead IPs).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Don't blanket-override TTLs — use unbound's cache-min-ttl: 300 (not 3600) as a floor, and respect upstream TTL as the ceiling. On connection-refused or TCP RST, invalidate the cache entry for that host (unbound-control flush) and re-resolve before retry. For known CDN ASNs, shorten the floor further (60s).
bottlenecks.detection: Metric tcp_connect_failure_rate per host correlated with dns_cache_age_seconds; alert when connect failures > 5% for a host whose cached record is > 10 min old. Sample periodic re-resolutions and compare against cached IP — alert on drift rate > 20% for top-1000 hosts.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a dedicated DNS resolver sits in this design For a web crawler targeting **~500 distinct hosts in flight at any moment** to sustain 400 pages/sec, every single fetch starts with a question: "what IP is `example.com`?" That question goes to DNS, and in most operating systems the resolver call is *synchronous* — the fetcher goroutine literally blocks waiting for an answer. A cold public DNS lookup costs 20–200ms, which is comparable to (or larger than) the actual HTTP fetch time. Without a local cache absorbing that cost, DNS becomes the single slowest step in the pipeline for popular hosts the crawler hits thousands of times a day. ## What happens without it Strip out the local unbound/dnsmasq cache and every fetch sends a query to a public resolver like 8.8.8.8. At 400 lookups/sec sustained, Google and Cloudflare will start rate-limiting your egress IP — you'll see `SERVFAIL` and `REFUSED` errors cascading into the fetcher, which then treats them as fetch failures. The operator watches fetcher throughput collapse from 400 pages/sec to under 100, while the frontier backs up into tens of millions of pending URLs because dequeues can't keep up. The fetcher component takes the visible hit, but the root cause is upstream. ## The arithmetic At 400 pages/sec with a 90% cache hit ratio, only 40 lookups/sec escape to upstream resolvers — comfortably under their rate limits. Drop the hit ratio to 50% and you're sending 200 qps upstream, which *will* get throttled. That's why the design specifies a 10M-entry cache with TTL overrides. ## Trade-off Overriding short TTLs up to 1 hour boosts the hit ratio but occasionally sends fetchers to stale IPs for CDN-fronted hosts whose IPs rotate every 60 seconds.

parser.name: Content Parser
parser.summary: Parses HTML, strips boilerplate, extracts text, and computes a SHA-256 of normalized content. Also validates that the page is well-formed (the book calls out invalid/malformed HTML as a real failure mode that wastes storage).

sections.heading: Why it's a separate service
sections.body: The book splits the parser from the downloader because parsing is slow and CPU-bound; bundling would block fetchers. Running it independently also lets us scale CPU separately from network.

sections.heading: Pipeline
sections.body:
1. Detect charset (meta / BOM / Content-Type)
2. Parse DOM (streaming with a SAX-style parser for speed)
3. Validate structure — malformed HTML wastes storage and is dropped
4. Extract main text (readability-style heuristics)
5. Normalize (lowercase, collapse whitespace, strip nav/footer)
6. Compute content_hash = SHA-256(normalized_text)
7. Emit text + hash downstream to 'Content Seen?' check

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Malformed HTML → parser should be permissive (browser-grade); fall back to regex for URL extraction on catastrophic failure.
- XML/PDF/JS-rendered sites → out of scope for MVP; route to specialized workers.

bottlenecks.title: CPU saturation from DOM parsing at sustained fetch rate
bottlenecks.trigger: Parser is CPU-bound at 20-80ms per page (per sim) and must sustain 400 pages/sec average with 1K peak. At p50 ~40ms that's 16 core-seconds/sec = 16 cores just for median parsing; at peak 1000 pages/sec with 80ms tail that's 80 cores. Median HTML is 120 KB but tail reaches 500 KB, and readability-style main-text extraction scales roughly linearly with DOM node count.
bottlenecks.symptom: Parser queue depth grows unbounded; fetcher throughput appears healthy but end-to-end pipeline lag climbs to minutes; CPU pinned at 100% on parser workers; p99 parser latency blows past 80ms into hundreds of ms; content-seen and URL-extractor downstream stages idle waiting for input.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Horizontally scale parser workers behind a work queue (Kafka or Redis streams) keyed by url_hash; target 2x headroom over peak (32+ cores for 1K peak). Use a streaming SAX-style parser (lxml/gumbo/html5ever in Rust via FFI) instead of building full DOM in memory. Cap per-page parse time at 2s hard timeout — abort and fall back to regex URL extraction on catastrophic HTML. Shed by routing pages > 2 MB to a separate 'heavy' pool.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric parser_cpu_utilization (alert > 75% 5-min avg); parser_queue_depth (alert > 10K pending); parser_latency_p99 (alert > 150ms); parser_timeout_rate (alert > 0.1%); track fetcher→parser lag as a wall-clock gauge.

bottlenecks.title: Malformed / adversarial HTML breaking the parser or inflating memory
bottlenecks.trigger: Parser sim reports 0.5% failure rate = ~2 failures/sec at 400 pages/sec = ~170K/day. Real-world HTML includes deeply nested tags (billion-laughs-style expansion), unclosed tags forcing DOM repair, and megabyte-of-whitespace pages. A single 10 MB (fetcher cap) page of pathological nesting can consume hundreds of MB of parser heap and pin a worker for seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Parser worker OOM-kills; GC pauses spike; a bad page causes the worker to crash and the in-flight batch to be re-processed on retry (possibly re-crashing); storage bill grows with 'successful' fetches that never reach the store; operator sees status='error' climbing in URL Storage.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run parser in a sandboxed subprocess with RLIMIT_AS (e.g. 512 MB) and RLIMIT_CPU (e.g. 2s) per page so a single bad page kills only its worker, not the pool. Use a permissive browser-grade parser (gumbo/html5ever) that never throws on malformed input. Validate pre-parse: reject if >1M DOM nodes estimated from byte size heuristics, or nesting depth >500. On parse exception, fall back to regex-based <a href> extraction so URL discovery still happens.
bottlenecks.detection: parser_oom_kills_total (alert > 0); parser_page_timeout_rate (alert > 0.1%); parser_fallback_regex_rate (alert > 1%); log sample of URLs causing failures and auto-blocklist hosts generating >100 failures/day.

bottlenecks.title: Charset misdetection producing garbage hashes and defeating content dedup
bottlenecks.trigger: Parser detects charset via meta/BOM/Content-Type and normalizes before SHA-256. When the declared charset disagrees with actual bytes (common on legacy CJK, Cyrillic, or mislabeled UTF-8 pages — probably 1-3% of the web), normalization produces different byte sequences for the same logical content. At 1B pages/mo with book-cited 29% duplicate rate, even 1% charset-induced hash divergence means ~3M duplicate pages/mo slip past the content-seen filter and get stored.
bottlenecks.symptom: Content-seen dedup ratio drops below the expected ~40%; storage grows faster than the 40 TB/mo budget; downstream index has near-duplicate entries for the same article; operators notice mirror sites producing 'new' hashes for pages already indexed under the canonical URL.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use chardet/uchardet for statistical charset detection when declared charset is absent or suspicious; always convert to canonical UTF-8 NFC before hashing. Normalize aggressively: NFKC unicode normalization, strip all HTML comments and script/style blocks before extracting text. For near-dup detection beyond exact hash, emit a SimHash (64-bit) alongside SHA-256 and dedupe on Hamming distance ≤ 3 in a follow-up pass.
bottlenecks.detection: Track content_seen_hit_ratio (alert if drops below 30% 7-day avg); sample 0.1% of 'new' hashes and compute SimHash similarity against recent hashes to estimate true near-dup rate; alert if estimated near-dup miss rate > 2%.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Content Parser lives here The crawler's goal isn't just to download HTML — it's to (1) detect duplicate *content* (the problem statement explicitly calls this out) and (2) discover new URLs to keep the frontier fed. Neither of those is possible on raw bytes. You need to extract the readable text to hash it, and you need a DOM walk to find `<a href>` links. The parser is where raw network bytes become structured data the rest of the pipeline can reason about. It's also deliberately split from the fetcher: fetching is IO-bound (waiting on slow servers), parsing is CPU-bound (chewing through 120 KB of tag soup), and bundling them would mean a slow-to-parse page blocks a fetcher goroutine that should be doing network work. ## What happens without it If you hashed raw HTML bytes directly, every page with a rotating ad banner or a different session ID in a hidden field would produce a unique hash — the content-seen dedupe ratio collapses from ~40% toward 0%, and suddenly you're storing 1.6B pages/month instead of 600M. The operator sees the storage bill balloon past the 40 TB/month budget, and the URL extractor — now starved of a clean DOM — falls back to brittle regex that misses half the outbound links, so frontier growth stalls. ## The number At 400 pages/sec sustained and 40ms median parse time, that's 400 × 0.040 = **16 cores pinned just on parsing**, rising to ~80 cores at the 1K/sec peak with 80ms tails. That's why parsing is a scalable worker pool, not a function call inside the fetcher. ## Trade-off Splitting parser from fetcher adds a queue hop and serialization cost, but it lets you scale CPU and network independently.

cseen.name: Content Seen? (hash store)
cseen.summary: Decision block + hash store. The book cites this as one of the key filters — ~29% of web pages are duplicates (it reports this statistic) and content-level dedupe reclaims that budget.

sections.heading: Why content-level dedupe
sections.body: Many URLs resolve to the same content (mirrors, redirects, session IDs in the URL, duplicated CDN copies). The book cites research that ~29% of pages on the web are duplicates. Content-hashing avoids paying to re-index the same bytes.

sections.heading: How
sections.body: Compare hash values of two pages rather than comparing characters — character-by-character is too slow at scale. Hash each page's normalized content and look up in the Content Seen store.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.body: Key = 32-byte SHA-256, value = first_seen_at. At 60% unique * 1B pages/mo = 600M new entries/mo → ~20 GB/mo. RocksDB or Cassandra with long TTLs.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.body: Exact-hash dedupe misses near-duplicates (same article with a different ad banner). For that you'd add SimHash / MinHash in a separate layer.

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from 600M new hashes/month plus dup-count updates
bottlenecks.trigger: At 400 pages/sec sustained (1K peak), cseen receives a GET+PUT per page. 60% unique = 240 PUTs/sec for new hashes; the other 40% (~160/sec) are duplicate hits that still update dup_count. Over a year that's 7.2B new keys (~230 GB raw) plus billions of in-place updates, driving RocksDB/Cassandra compactions hard.
bottlenecks.symptom: Parser-side latency p99 on cseen GET climbs from 10ms into 50-100ms during compaction windows; write stalls show up as periodic throughput dips; storage tier reports growing pending compaction bytes; dup_count updates lag behind real-time.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use RocksDB with universal compaction and a dedicated column family for hash→metadata; size memtable to 512 MB and enable rate-limited compaction (50 MB/s). Drop dup_count updates from the hot path — increment a separate counter via async batch writer, or skip entirely if only first_seen matters. Shard by hash prefix across 8+ nodes so per-node write rate stays under 50 PUTs/sec.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cseen_put_latency_p99 > 30ms, rocksdb_pending_compaction_bytes > 10 GB, and write_stall_micros > 0. Track PUT rate vs. compaction throughput ratio — if PUT rate > 80% of compaction throughput, scale out.

bottlenecks.title: Exact-hash dedup misses near-duplicates, defeating the 29% duplicate budget
bottlenecks.trigger: The book cites ~29% of web pages as duplicates, but SHA-256 of normalized text only catches bytes-identical content. Pages with rotating ads, personalized recommendations, A/B-tested layouts, timestamp/counter widgets, or CSRF tokens produce different hashes for semantically identical content. Realistic near-dup rate is 10-20% of pages that slip past exact hashing.
bottlenecks.symptom: Content storage grows faster than the 40 TB/month budget (possibly 50-55 TB); downstream index shows multiple near-identical entries for the same article; operators notice mirror sites producing new hashes despite the page being indexed under a canonical URL; dedup ratio stays below the 40% target.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a parallel SimHash (64-bit) or MinHash LSH tier alongside SHA-256. On cseen miss, also query the SimHash index with Hamming distance ≤ 3; if a near-dup is found, record as duplicate with canonical pointer. Aggressive pre-hash normalization: strip script/style, NFKC unicode normalization, remove all numbers and URLs from text, drop short blocks (likely nav/ads).
bottlenecks.detection: Sample 0.1% of 'new' hashes daily and compute SimHash similarity against the last 30 days of hashes — alert if estimated near-dup miss rate > 5%. Track content_storage_growth_rate vs. new_hash_rate — divergence indicates near-dup leakage. Dashboard: dedup_ratio 7-day avg (alert < 35%).

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded hash set growth with no eviction or tiering strategy
bottlenecks.trigger: At 600M new entries/month (60% of 1B unique pages), after 2 years cseen holds ~14.4B rows. At 32-byte key + 40-byte value + index overhead ≈ 100 bytes/row, that's ~1.4 TB of hot data — too large to cache fully in RAM, forcing more reads to hit disk/SSD. Each cseen GET becomes a disk seek on tail hashes.
bottlenecks.symptom: cseen GET p99 latency drifts upward over months (10ms → 30ms → 80ms); cache hit ratio on the hash KV drops below 70%; parser throughput ceiling lowers as cseen becomes the pipeline bottleneck; SSD IOPS on the cseen cluster saturates.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier by recency: keep last 90 days of hashes in hot RocksDB (fits in ~50 GB, cacheable in RAM), move older hashes to cold storage (S3 + sorted file per month) queried only on cache miss. Alternatively apply TTL of 12-18 months on the assumption that a page re-discovered after that long is worth re-crawling. Bloom filter in front of the cold tier to avoid unnecessary cold lookups.
bottlenecks.detection: Track cseen_total_rows growth, cseen_get_latency_p99 by key-age bucket (alert if p99 for keys > 90 days old exceeds 50ms), cseen_cache_hit_ratio (alert < 80%), and SSD IOPS utilization (alert > 70%).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Content-Seen lives in this crawler The problem statement says the crawler must avoid **both URL-level and content-level duplicates**. URL-level dedupe is handled upstream by the Bloom filter — but that only catches cases where we see the exact same URL twice. The web is full of situations where *different* URLs serve *identical* content: CDN mirrors, session IDs baked into the path, tracking parameters, syndicated articles, redirect chains. The URL-seen filter can't catch any of that because the URL strings genuinely differ. Content-seen is the second line of defense: after we've already paid to fetch and parse the page, we hash its normalized text and check "have I indexed these bytes before?" If yes, we skip storing it (but still mine its outbound links). ## What happens without it Strip this component out and the Content Storage bill explodes. The book cites research that roughly **29% of web pages are duplicates** — without content-seen, we'd be paying to store 1.29× the unique content. Operators see storage growth outrun the budget, the downstream index gets polluted with mirror copies of the same article under dozens of URLs, and ML/search teams downstream have to do the dedup work themselves at query time. ## The number At 1B pages/mo and 40 KB compressed per page = **40 TB/mo storage budget**. If 29% are duplicates and we skip storing them, we save 40 TB × 0.29 ≈ **11.6 TB/month** — roughly 140 TB/year of S3 not bought. ## Trade-off Exact SHA-256 matching misses near-duplicates (same article, different ad banner). The designer accepted that gap, leaving SimHash/MinHash as a future layer.

extractor.name: URL Extractor
extractor.summary: Pulls outbound , , URLs from the parsed DOM.

sections.heading: Normalization
sections.body:
- Resolve relative URLs against the base URL
- Strip fragments (#section)
- Sort query params deterministically
- Lowercase scheme + host
Normalization improves URL-seen hit ratio dramatically.

sections.heading: Outputs
sections.body: A deduplicated list of absolute URLs, tagged with the source page's URL and depth.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Relative URL tricks (javascript:, data:) → blacklist schemes
- Very long URLs → cap at 2048 chars

bottlenecks.title: URL normalization CPU cost at fanout rate
bottlenecks.trigger: At 400 pages/sec sustained (1K peak) with an average of ~47 outbound links per page (per happy-path op), the extractor must normalize ~18,800 URLs/sec average and ~47,000/sec at peak. Each URL requires urljoin, scheme/host lowercasing, fragment strip, query-param sort, and length cap — roughly 5-20μs per URL. At peak that's 0.25-0.95 core-seconds/sec just on normalization, plus DOM selector traversal on pages up to 500 KB.
bottlenecks.symptom: Extractor queue depth grows during peak bursts; p99 per-page latency climbs from 20ms into 100ms+; parser→extractor lag becomes visible as end-to-end pipeline delay; downstream filter and useen stages idle waiting for batches; CPU on extractor workers pinned at 100%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Scale horizontally behind the same work queue as parser (keyed by url_hash); co-locate extractor with parser to avoid DOM re-serialization (pass parsed DOM in-process, not re-parse). Use a compiled regex/URL library (e.g. Rust `url` crate via FFI, or Go `net/url` with custom fast path) instead of Python urllib. Batch-normalize URLs in SIMD-friendly buffers. Target 2x headroom over peak (~2 cores minimum per worker, scaled to 8+ for 1K peak).
bottlenecks.detection: extractor_urls_per_sec (alert if sustained > 40K/sec without scale-out), extractor_latency_p99 (alert > 50ms), extractor_queue_depth (alert > 5K pending), extractor_cpu_utilization (alert > 75% 5-min avg).

bottlenecks.title: Link-farm / hub pages producing pathological fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: Average page has ~47 outbound links but sitemap indexes, link directories, and spam link farms can contain 10K-100K <a href> tags per page. A single such page at 100K links × 20μs normalization = 2s of CPU pinned on one worker, and injects 100K URLs downstream into the filter/useen pipeline in one burst. At 400 pages/sec, even 1-in-10K pages being a link farm means ~5 such bursts/min.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sporadic extractor latency spikes into seconds for specific URLs; downstream filter and useen see bursty load patterns (10K+ URL batches) that blow through their concurrency windows; frontier enqueue rate briefly spikes 100x baseline; one worker stalls while others idle; memory spike on extractor worker holding the giant link list.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap links extracted per page at 1000 (truncate with a warning metric — real content pages rarely exceed this). Stream link extraction rather than buffering full list, so memory stays bounded. Detect link-farm pattern (>5000 outbound to distinct hosts, or >1000 to same host) and auto-add source host to blocklist review queue. Rate-limit per-page outbound URLs to downstream stages via a token bucket (e.g. max 500 URLs/page pushed per second).
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram of outbound_links_per_page with alert on p99.9 > 2000; extractor_pages_truncated_total counter (alert if > 100/hour); per-source-host outbound_link_rate with daily top-20 report reviewed by on-call; memory_rss per extractor worker (alert on spikes > 2GB).

bottlenecks.title: Parametric URL explosion defeating normalization and inflating frontier
bottlenecks.trigger: Normalization sorts query params deterministically, but does NOT remove tracking params (utm_*, fbclid, gclid, session IDs, timestamps). A single page linking to /product?id=123&utm_source=a vs /product?id=123&utm_source=b produces 2 'unique' normalized URLs for the same resource. Across 1B pages/month with ~5-10% of outbound links carrying tracking params, this injects 100M+ spurious URLs/month that all pass useen as 'new' and waste frontier slots, fetcher cycles, and content-seen bandwidth (only caught after full fetch).
bottlenecks.symptom: Frontier size grows faster than crawled-pages rate; content-seen dedup ratio climbs well above the expected 40% (same content fetched under tracking variants); per-host URL counts inflate (hitting the 100K/host/day quota on hosts that really only have 10K distinct resources); storage and bandwidth budgets strain.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a tracking-param blocklist (utm_*, fbclid, gclid, mc_cid, _ga, ref, session, sid, timestamp, etc.) stripped during normalization. Apply URL template clustering: replace runs of digits with \d+ for per-host cardinality detection; if a host produces >1K URLs matching a single template, treat template as parametric and sample-crawl instead of exhaustive. Honor <link rel="canonical"> from the parser when available to collapse variants before extraction output.
bottlenecks.detection: Track unique_url_to_unique_content_ratio (alert if > 1.5 — means normalization is leaking variants); per-host template cardinality metric (alert on hosts with single-template URL count > 1K/day); monitor content-seen hit ratio by source host to spot worst offenders.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the URL Extractor is here A web crawler is only as big as the set of URLs it knows about. The seed list gets you started with maybe tens of thousands of hosts, but the problem statement demands ingesting **billions of URLs** — those URLs have to come from somewhere, and that somewhere is the outbound `<a href>` links on every page the crawler fetches. The Extractor is the component that turns each fetched page into 30–50 new candidate URLs, feeding the frontier so the whole pipeline keeps running. Without it, the crawler would drain its seed list in minutes and go idle. ## What happens without it If you removed the Extractor, the fetcher, parser, and storage pipeline would all look healthy for a short burst — then the frontier would empty out and 500 fetcher goroutines per worker would sit idle waiting for work that never arrives. The operator sees `frontier_size` collapse to zero, `fetcher_hosts_in_flight` drop toward single digits, and throughput fall from 400 pages/sec to nothing. The crawler has effectively become a one-shot fetcher of its seed list. ## The number At 400 pages/sec sustained with ~47 outbound links per page, the Extractor emits ~18,800 URLs/sec into the downstream filter and useen stages. Even after filtering and dedupe (where most get dropped as already-seen), the net *new* URLs per page needs to average just over 1 to keep the frontier from shrinking — 47 links gives plenty of headroom for the 40% duplicate rate and per-host quotas. ## Trade-off Normalization (lowercasing hosts, sorting query params, stripping fragments) burns CPU on every link, but without it the URL-seen dedupe ratio collapses and the frontier fills with trivial variants of the same page.

filter.name: URL Filter (robots + blocklist)
filter.summary: Applies robots.txt rules, host blocklist, scheme whitelist, and quota caps.

sections.heading: Rule pipeline
sections.body:
1. Scheme allowed? (http, https only)
2. Host blocklisted? (spam, malware, CSAM lists)
3. Path allowed by robots.txt?
4. Per-host quota remaining? (e.g. max 100K URLs/host/day)
5. Depth limit? (default 10 from seed)

sections.heading: robots.txt cache
sections.body: Rulesets cached from the fetcher layer. Filter consults the same local cache — no extra network hop.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- robots.txt 404 → treat as 'allow all' per RFC
- robots.txt 5xx → treat as 'disallow all' for a short period (polite default)

bottlenecks.title: robots.txt cache miss storm on new-host discovery
bottlenecks.trigger: At 400 pages/sec with ~47 outbound links/page, the extractor emits ~18,800 URLs/sec into the filter. When BFS discovers new hosts in bursts (10K+ new hosts/day baseline, spiking on hub pages), each first URL per host triggers a robots.txt fetch. A single fan-out page linking to 1000 new hosts causes 1000 synchronous robots fetches, each 20-500ms, before any of those URLs can be evaluated.
bottlenecks.symptom: Filter p99 latency jumps from 5ms to seconds on new-host bursts; filter queue depth climbs into hundreds of thousands; useen and frontier enqueue rates stall; fetcher pool drains because no new URLs reach the frontier; tail of new hosts sit in 'pending robots fetch' state for minutes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Decouple robots.txt fetch from the filter hot path: on cache miss, push URL to a 'pending-robots' holding queue, async-fetch robots.txt, and re-admit the URL once rules are cached. Pre-warm robots cache at URL Frontier enqueue time (not at filter time). Set negative-cache TTL of 15 min for robots.txt 5xx/timeout (treat as disallow-all per design) to avoid retry storms. Shard robots cache across filter workers with consistent hashing on host.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric robots_cache_hit_ratio (alert < 95%); filter_pending_robots_queue_depth (alert > 10K); filter_latency_p99 (alert > 20ms); filter_throughput vs. extractor_output_rate divergence (alert if filter throughput < 80% of input for >2min).

bottlenecks.title: Per-host quota counter contention under skewed link graph
bottlenecks.trigger: Filter enforces per-host quotas (e.g. 100K URLs/host/day) which requires an atomic increment+check per URL. With ~18,800 URLs/sec flowing through and hot hosts (wikipedia.org, youtube.com) receiving thousands of URL fan-ins per second from BFS concentration, the quota counter for top hosts becomes a write hotspot. If counters live in Redis/Cassandra, a single hot host can see 5000+ INCR/sec against one key.
bottlenecks.symptom: Filter latency bimodal — fast for cold hosts, slow (20-100ms) for hot hosts; Redis CPU pegged on specific keys; hot shards in the quota KV report elevated p99; quota decisions occasionally race (two workers both see 99,999 and both admit, overshooting daily cap by dozens).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use local in-process counters per filter worker with periodic (every 1000 URLs or 1s) sync to a central Redis counter via INCRBY batches — trade exact precision for throughput. Alternatively use approximate counting (CMS sketch) for quota enforcement. Shard quota keys by host+bucket (e.g. host:hour) to spread writes. For the top-1K hottest hosts, cache counter locally with TTL and check centrally only near the quota boundary.
bottlenecks.detection: redis_key_hotness per quota key (alert on any key > 1000 ops/sec); filter_quota_check_latency_p99 by host (alert > 15ms); daily report of hosts exceeding quota by >5% (indicates race conditions); quota counter sync lag metric (alert > 5s).

bottlenecks.title: Stale blocklist and robots cache missing fresh abuse / policy changes
bottlenecks.trigger: Design caches robots.txt rulesets with 24h TTL and uses a static domain blocklist loaded at startup. When a site updates robots.txt to disallow paths (e.g. after a news story triggers takedown demand) or a host is newly flagged as malware/CSAM, the filter continues admitting URLs for up to 24h. At 400 pages/sec, that's potentially millions of URLs fetched against stale rules.
bottlenecks.symptom: Site owner complaint tickets for crawling disallowed paths; legal escalation from fetching blocklisted content; security team flags crawler IP as touching known-bad domains; post-incident review shows robots.txt updated X hours before offending fetches.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shorten robots.txt cache TTL to 1-4h for actively-crawled hosts (they're in memory anyway, re-fetch cost is small). Subscribe filter workers to a pub/sub channel (Redis pub/sub, Kafka compacted topic) that broadcasts blocklist updates and robots.txt invalidations in real time. Support operator-triggered cache flush per host via admin API. Honor short Cache-Control headers on robots.txt when present instead of blanket 24h.
bottlenecks.detection: Track robots_cache_age_seconds p95 (alert > 4h); blocklist_version_skew across filter workers (alert on any worker > 5min behind latest); audit log sampling 0.01% of admitted URLs against current blocklist/robots to detect enforcement drift; alert on any fetch of a URL whose host appeared on blocklist > 1min before fetch timestamp.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the URL Filter is here The problem statement has one word that makes this component non-negotiable: **polite**. A crawler ingesting billions of URLs is, by default, indistinguishable from a DDoS attack — and the web's social contract for what's off-limits is written in each host's `/robots.txt`. The Filter is the single chokepoint where the crawler says "*before I add this URL to the frontier, is it even legal for me to fetch?*" It also enforces the host blocklist (malware, CSAM, known spam traps), scheme whitelist (no `javascript:` or `data:` URLs leaking in from the extractor), and per-host daily quotas that keep a single mega-site from monopolizing the frontier. ## What happens without it Strip the Filter out and the crawler becomes impolite overnight. Webmasters notice first: their logs show your crawler hammering `/admin/` and `/private/` paths that `robots.txt` explicitly disallowed. Complaints escalate, your egress IPs land on abuse lists, and the fetcher starts seeing a wave of 403s and WAF blocks. Meanwhile the frontier fills with garbage — `mailto:` links, calendar-trap URLs going to year 9999, blocklisted malware hosts — and the useen Bloom filter gets polluted with URLs that should never have been considered in the first place. ## The numbers At 400 pages/sec with ~47 outbound links per page, the extractor emits **~18,800 URLs/sec** into the Filter. Catching disallowed URLs *here* — before they hit useen's Bloom filter, URL Storage, and eventually the fetcher — is vastly cheaper than catching them after a wasted TCP connection and TLS handshake downstream. ## Trade-off The Filter adds a mandatory hop on every URL (1–5ms) and depends on a fresh robots.txt cache — stale rules can briefly allow URLs the site owner just disallowed.

useen.name: URL Seen? (Bloom filter + URL Storage)
useen.summary: Two-tier dedupe check: in-RAM Bloom filter fast path, plus persistent URL Storage as truth. Keeps the crawler from adding already-visited or already-enqueued URLs back to the frontier.

sections.heading: Why
sections.body: The book notes: helps avoid adding the same URL to the frontier multiple times (which would waste crawler cycles and potentially cause infinite loops on cyclic links). Also prevents re-visiting known URLs.

sections.heading: Bloom filter tier
sections.body:
- ~12 GB RAM per crawler, 10^10 entries, ~1% false positive rate
- BloomFilter.mightContain(url) → False means DEFINITELY not seen; True means probably seen
- False positives cause us to rarely skip a URL we haven't actually seen — acceptable
- Book explicitly mentions Bloom filter / hash table as the data structures for this check.

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body: Both tiers updated atomically: BloomFilter.add(url); ustore.put(hash(url), first_seen_at). The Bloom filter is periodically snapshotted so a restart doesn't lose 12 GB of in-memory state.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Bloom filter corrupted → load snapshot; warm up from URL Storage.
- URL Storage lag behind Bloom → rare; write Bloom second if ordering matters.

gained: Slightly better FPR at same bit budget
Simpler; no RAM tier to operate
lost: Every URL triggers a DB round trip → 5-10x higher load on the KV

bottlenecks.title: Bloom filter RAM cap breached as URL set grows past 10^10
bottlenecks.trigger: Design sizes the Bloom filter at 10^10 entries × 10 bits = ~12 GB for 1% FPR. At 1B pages/mo crawled with ~3x discovered:crawled fanout (~3B URLs/mo entering useen), the filter hits 10^10 insertions in ~3-4 months and then keeps growing. Beyond design capacity, FPR climbs non-linearly — at 2x load (2×10^10 entries in 12 GB) FPR jumps from 1% to ~10%.
bottlenecks.symptom: URL-seen dedupe ratio drops as false positives force DB lookups — DB QPS jumps from ~20% of useen calls (Bloom miss path) to 50%+; useen p99 climbs from 4ms to 20ms+; fetcher throughput dips because frontier ingest is slower; operators see genuinely-new URLs being dropped as 'already seen' when DB lookup is skipped on the fast path.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Scale Bloom filter by sharding across multiple crawler workers (each shard owns a hash range, ~10^10 entries per shard, 12 GB RAM per shard). Use a scalable/layered Bloom design (e.g. Bloom filter cascade — add a new layer when the current one passes its target FPR, keep old layers read-only). Alternative: switch to a counting Cuckoo filter which handles deletion and ages out URLs older than N months. Always fall through to DB on Bloom hit (never trust Bloom alone for 'seen=true').
bottlenecks.detection: Track bloom_cardinality vs capacity (alert when >80% of 10^10); measured_false_positive_rate sampled by cross-checking 0.1% of Bloom hits against DB (alert >2%); useen_db_lookup_rate (alert on rising trend indicating more Bloom hits); useen_p99_latency (alert >10ms).

bottlenecks.title: Bloom filter state loss on crash forcing full DB warmup
bottlenecks.trigger: Bloom filter is in-memory (~12 GB). A process crash, OOM-kill, or node replacement wipes it entirely. Without a warm snapshot, every subsequent URL check must fall through to URL Storage DB. At ~18,800 URLs/sec entering useen (400 pages/sec × 47 links/page), a cold Bloom means 18.8K DB GETs/sec against a 300 GB/mo growing KV — 5-10x normal DB load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-restart spike in URL Storage DB CPU and p99 latency (3-10ms normal → 50-200ms under cold load); useen throughput collapses from 10K concurrent to hundreds; frontier ingest rate drops, back queues drain faster than they fill, fetcher pool idles; warmup to steady-state takes hours as Bloom slowly repopulates from DB scans.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Snapshot Bloom filter to disk every 5 min (mmap-backed file or periodic serialization to S3 — 12 GB compressed ~3-4 GB, fast to restore). On startup, load most recent snapshot, then replay URL Storage writes since snapshot timestamp from a WAL/Kafka topic. Run useen workers with restart policies that prefer snapshot-restore over cold init. Keep a secondary hot replica of the Bloom filter behind the same hash range for instant failover.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric useen_bloom_snapshot_age_seconds (alert >10 min); useen_cold_start_in_progress flag with alert if set >2 min; DB-side alert on urlstorage_get_rate spike >3x baseline; track useen_bloom_hit_ratio (alert if drops below 95% — indicates cold or corrupted filter).

bottlenecks.title: Dual-write race between Bloom and URL Storage on concurrent duplicate URLs
bottlenecks.trigger: useen writes both Bloom (bloom.add) and DB (ustore.put) on every new URL. With 10K concurrent workers and BFS naturally producing the same URL from multiple source pages near-simultaneously (e.g. a popular hub linked from 50 pages in flight), two workers can both observe Bloom=miss, both write to DB, and both enqueue the URL to the frontier — causing duplicate fetches and wasted politeness budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Frontier contains duplicate entries for popular URLs; same URL fetched 2-5x within minutes; content-seen dedup ratio climbs above expected ~40% (second fetch hits content-seen); per-host quota consumed faster than expected; operators spot duplicate fetch_ts entries in URL Storage for the same url_hash.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use conditional write (DB putIfAbsent / INSERT IF NOT EXISTS on url_hash PK) as the authoritative dedup — only enqueue to frontier if the write was the first one. Bloom stays as a fast-path filter but never as the commit point. Alternatively partition useen by url_hash so a given URL is always handled by one worker (consistent hashing), eliminating the race. Batch incoming URLs in 10ms windows and dedupe within the batch before hitting the tier.
bottlenecks.detection: DB-side metric urlstorage_conditional_write_conflict_rate (alert >0.5%); sample frontier for duplicate url_hash entries (alert on any found in a 5-min window); correlate fetch_log by url_hash for duplicate fetches within 1h (alert >0.1% of fetches).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why URL-Seen lives in this crawler The problem statement requires avoiding **URL-level duplicates** — and without that check, BFS on the web graph becomes a nightmare. Every page links back to other pages (think of how many sites link to `wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page`), so the Extractor emits URLs the crawler has already processed *constantly*. If those re-discovered URLs went straight back into the frontier, the crawler would fetch the same pages over and over, blow past per-host politeness budgets, and might get stuck in a cyclic link loop forever. URL-Seen is the gate between "URL that passed filtering" and "URL that actually gets enqueued for a fetch." ## What happens without it Strip useen out and the frontier grows unboundedly while the *unique* pages crawled stays flat. The operator sees fetcher throughput collapse — workers are re-fetching pages they already stored, the politeness back-queues for popular hosts balloon with duplicates, and content-seen downstream catches the duplication too late (after paying for a full TCP+TLS+download cycle). Storage keeps growing with redundant WARC entries, and the 400 pages/sec target becomes 400 *re-fetches*/sec of the same neighborhood. ## The numbers At 1B pages/month with ~3x discovered:crawled fanout, useen sees roughly **18,800 URL checks/sec**. If every one hit URL Storage directly, that's 18.8K DB GETs/sec against a 300 GB+ KV — expensive and slow (5–20ms per lookup). The Bloom filter handles that in ~200ns of RAM for the ~99% case where the URL is definitely new, so only real hits fall through to the DB. That's ~12 GB of RAM to save ~90% of DB QPS. ## Trade-off The 1% Bloom false-positive rate occasionally tells us a genuinely-new URL is "probably seen," so we rarely skip a URL we should have crawled — the designer accepted that silent loss for the RAM-scale speedup.

store.name: Content Storage
store.summary: Compressed HTML archive + extracted text, for downstream indexing / ML. The book recommends a hybrid: popular/hot content in memory, the bulk on disk.

sections.heading: Storage tiering (book)
sections.body: Most HTML content is kept on disk because the dataset is too big for memory (petabyte-scale). Popular content is cached in memory to cut read latency. Writes append to disk as pages arrive.

sections.heading: Format
sections.body: WARC files (Web ARChive — the standard format used by IA and Common Crawl), ~1 GB per file, gzipped. Object storage (S3/GCS) with Glacier tiering after 90 days.

sections.heading: Metadata
sections.body: A separate index (Parquet or Cassandra) maps url → {warc_file, byte_offset, length, content_hash, fetch_ts}.

sections.heading: Volume
sections.body: 40 TB/month → ~40 000 WARC files/month. Trivially partitioned by date prefix.

bottlenecks.title: S3 PUT rate saturation from per-page object writes
bottlenecks.trigger: At 400 pages/sec sustained (1K peak), if each page is written as an individual S3 object the store faces 400-1000 PUT/sec. S3 prefix partitions soft-cap at 3500 PUT/sec but sustained high rates on a single date prefix (e.g. cc-2026-04-24-*) trigger 503 SlowDown responses. Writing 1B objects/mo also inflates request cost ($5/1M PUTs = $5K/mo) separately from storage cost.
bottlenecks.symptom: S3 returns 503 SlowDown errors during peak bursts; write p99 climbs from 50ms into seconds; parser→store backpressure propagates upstream causing parser queue depth growth; AWS bill shows request charges dominating storage charges; WARC writer exceptions in logs during hour-boundary traffic spikes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch pages into 1 GB WARC files (already specified) with in-memory buffering — one PUT per ~25K pages instead of per page. Shard WARC writers across multiple prefixes (hash of url_hash → shard_id) to spread across S3 partitions; use random hex prefix instead of date-first prefix to maximize partition parallelism. Run 4-8 WARC writer workers in parallel, each owning a prefix shard. Use S3 multipart upload for WARCs >100 MB to pipeline write with ongoing page ingestion.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on s3_put_5xx_rate > 0.1%, s3_slowdown_errors > 0 in any 1-min window; track warc_writer_buffer_flush_latency_p99 (alert > 500ms); monitor PUT count vs. page count ratio (alert if > 1 PUT per 10K pages — indicates batching broken); dashboard S3 request cost vs. storage cost ratio weekly.

bottlenecks.title: Metadata index hotspot on url→WARC-location lookups
bottlenecks.trigger: The metadata index (Parquet or Cassandra) grows by ~1B rows/month mapping url_hash → {warc_file, byte_offset, length, content_hash, fetch_ts}. At 400 writes/sec sustained plus downstream indexers reading for re-crawl scheduling and freshness checks, the index sees both write and read pressure. At 60 bytes/row × 1B rows = ~60 GB/month of index growth, reaching ~720 GB/year — exceeding single-node Cassandra memory cache and pushing reads to disk.
bottlenecks.symptom: Metadata writes lag behind WARC appends (races where operator queries a page whose WARC is written but metadata isn't); p99 metadata GET latency climbs from 5ms to 50ms+ as index size outgrows RAM cache; re-crawl scheduler slows because last_fetched lookups become the bottleneck; Cassandra compaction pressure on the metadata table.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard the metadata index by url_hash prefix across 8+ Cassandra nodes; use LeveledCompactionStrategy tuned for read-heavy workload. Partition by fetch month (metadata_2026_04) so hot recent data stays in RAM and old months archive to cold Parquet on S3 queried only via Athena/Presto. Batch metadata writes (1000 rows per commit) to amortize WAL. Keep a secondary Bloom-filter tier on the metadata table to short-circuit reads for missing URLs.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric metadata_get_latency_p99 (alert > 30ms); metadata_write_lag_behind_warc_append_seconds (alert > 10s); cassandra_cache_hit_ratio by table (alert < 80% on metadata table); track metadata_index_size_gb growth and alert when approaching per-node RAM limit.

bottlenecks.title: WARC writer durability gap risks data loss on worker crash
bottlenecks.trigger: WARC files buffer ~1 GB (~25K pages) in memory before flushing to S3. At 400 pages/sec, that's a ~60-second buffer window. A WARC writer crash, OOM-kill, or graceful shutdown without proper flush drops up to 25K already-fetched pages — and upstream (fetcher, parser, useen) has already marked those URLs as crawled, so they won't be re-fetched.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-incident page count in Content Storage is less than successful fetch count in fetcher metrics; downstream index has missing pages for URLs marked 'crawled' in URL Storage; operators report holes in the corpus after node replacements; content-seen DB contains hashes with no corresponding WARC entry (dangling references).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use S3 multipart upload with part size 16 MB — flush parts as soon as filled so in-flight data loss caps at ~16 MB (~400 pages) not 1 GB. Write a local WAL on attached SSD before acknowledging the write to parser, so a crash can replay unwritten pages to S3 on restart. Delay marking URL as 'crawled' in URL Storage until the WARC commit completes (two-phase: fetched → stored). Run WARC writers with SIGTERM handlers that force-flush before exit.
bottlenecks.detection: Reconciliation job comparing fetch_success_count vs. warc_pages_written_count hourly (alert on divergence > 0.1%); warc_writer_unflushed_pages gauge (alert > 5000); content_seen_dangling_hash_rate sampled daily (alert > 0.01%); track warc_multipart_upload_pending_parts (alert on any part > 5 min old).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Content Storage lives in this crawler The whole point of crawling the web is to *keep* what you fetched — otherwise you've just burned 80 MB/s of bandwidth for nothing. Downstream consumers (search indexers, ML training pipelines, analytics jobs) need to read the raw HTML and extracted text long after the crawl happened, often multiple times, and usually in bulk batch jobs rather than one-page-at-a-time. Content Storage is the durable archive that decouples the *write-once, high-throughput* crawl pipeline from the *read-many, whenever-you-want* consumer workloads. The crawler doesn't know or care who will read the pages; it just needs to append them somewhere cheap, compressed, and effectively infinite. ## What happens without it Strip this out and the pipeline has nowhere to put the parsed HTML. Either the parser blocks (backing up into the fetcher, which backs up into the frontier, which stalls at ~18M pending URLs), or pages get dropped on the floor and the crawl produces nothing useful. The operator sees a healthy-looking fetch rate but an empty corpus; the search team downstream has no input; the content-seen dedup check still works but is pointless because there's no stored page behind the hash. ## The number At 1B pages/month × 40 KB compressed per page = **40 TB/month**, or ~500 TB/year. That's squarely in object-storage territory (S3/GCS) — you can't fit this in Postgres or Redis, and you don't want to pay SSD prices for data that's read in monthly batches. WARC files of ~1 GB each means ~40,000 files/month, trivially partitioned by date prefix. ## Trade-off Object storage gives you cheap petabyte-scale writes but read latency of 50–100ms per object — fine for batch, painful for interactive lookups, which is why a separate metadata index maps URL → WARC offset.

ustore.name: URL Storage
ustore.summary: Persistent record of every URL the crawler has ever decided to process — whether crawled successfully, blocked by robots, or dropped by filter. Source of truth for the 'URL Seen?' check when the Bloom filter reports a maybe-hit.

sections.heading: Data model
sections.body:
```
TABLE url_seen url_hash BIGINT PRIMARY KEY -- 64-bit xxhash of normalized URL url TEXT first_seen TIMESTAMP status TEXT -- 'crawled' | 'robots_blocked' | 'filtered' | 'error' last_fetched TIMESTAMP
```

sections.heading: Scale
sections.body: At 1B pages/month and ~3x discovered:crawled ratio, the URL Seen set grows by ~3B entries/month. At 100 bytes/row that's ~300 GB/month — RocksDB or Cassandra sharded by `url_hash` handles this comfortably.

sections.heading: Why separate from the Bloom filter
sections.body: Bloom filter is probabilistic and in-memory — fast but loses data on crash and cannot answer 'what's the first_seen timestamp?'. URL Storage provides durability and metadata for operators + freshness scheduling.

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from 3B URL inserts/month hitting LSM compaction
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1B pages/mo crawled with ~3x discovered:crawled fanout, ustore ingests ~3B new rows/month = ~1160 PUTs/sec sustained, ~3000/sec peak. Each row is ~100 bytes + secondary index overhead, adding ~300 GB/month to the table. RocksDB/Cassandra LSM compaction amplifies writes 10-30x — at 1160 PUTs/sec that's effectively 10K+ disk writes/sec driving sustained compaction pressure.
bottlenecks.symptom: ustore PUT p99 climbs from 10ms into 50-200ms during compaction windows; useen Bloom-false-positive path (which falls through to ustore) sees latency spikes; frontier enqueue rate lags extractor output rate; disk I/O saturated on ustore nodes; pending_compaction_bytes grows unboundedly.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard ustore by url_hash prefix across 8+ nodes so per-node PUT rate stays under 200/sec. Use RocksDB with universal compaction, 512 MB memtables, and rate-limited compaction (50 MB/sec). Batch PUTs from useen workers in 100-row batches to amortize WAL fsync. Consider Cassandra with LeveledCompactionStrategy if read-heavy (freshness scheduler queries dominate).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ustore_put_latency_p99 > 30ms, rocksdb_pending_compaction_bytes > 10 GB per node, write_stall_micros > 0; track PUT rate vs. compaction throughput ratio (alert if PUT rate > 70% of compaction throughput).

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded growth past 36B rows/year with no tiering
bottlenecks.trigger: At ~3B new rows/month (discovered URLs, not just crawled), ustore grows by ~300 GB/month. After 1 year that's 36B rows / ~3.6 TB; after 2 years, 72B rows / ~7 TB. This exceeds per-node RAM cache on any single Cassandra/RocksDB node, pushing reads to disk. The useen Bloom-false-positive path (~1% of ~18,800 URL checks/sec = ~188 GETs/sec) starts hitting cold SSD rather than page cache.
