bottlenecks.symptom: ustore GET p99 drifts upward over months (5ms → 30ms → 100ms); cache hit ratio drops below 70%; useen total latency climbs as more Bloom hits fall through to increasingly slow DB lookups; frontier ingest throughput ceiling drops; disk space alerts; backup/restore times become unmanageable.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier by recency: keep last 90 days hot in RocksDB/Cassandra (~900 GB, cacheable across a sharded fleet), archive older rows to cold Parquet on S3 queried via Athena/Presto for freshness-scheduler backfills. Apply TTL of 18 months on the assumption a URL re-discovered after that long is worth re-evaluating. Partition hot table by month (url_seen_2026_04) so queries hit only relevant shards.
bottlenecks.detection: Track ustore_total_rows and ustore_size_gb with growth-rate alerts; ustore_get_latency_p99 bucketed by row-age (alert if p99 for rows > 90 days old exceeds 50ms); ustore_cache_hit_ratio (alert < 80%); SSD utilization per node (alert > 70%).

bottlenecks.title: Hot-partition contention on popular URL hashes from concurrent BFS fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: useen has 10K concurrent workers. BFS naturally discovers the same popular URL (e.g. wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Page) from many source pages near-simultaneously — the happy-path op shows 18,800 URLs/sec through useen with 13 of 43 per batch being Bloom-hits that consult ustore. Popular URLs receive dozens of concurrent GET+conditional-PUT attempts within milliseconds, hitting the same row/partition.
bottlenecks.symptom: Row-level write conflicts and retries on hot url_hash keys; Cassandra reports elevated read-repair or LWT contention; duplicate url_hash rows briefly appear with different first_seen timestamps (race losers); useen sometimes enqueues the same URL twice to the frontier, wasting politeness budget; p99 PUT latency bimodal (fast for cold keys, 50ms+ for hot keys).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use putIfAbsent / INSERT IF NOT EXISTS (Cassandra LWT or RocksDB merge operator) so only the first writer wins and subsequent writers short-circuit. Partition useen workers by url_hash via consistent hashing so a given URL is always owned by one worker — eliminates cross-worker race entirely. Batch incoming URLs in 10ms windows and dedupe within batch before hitting ustore.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric ustore_conditional_write_conflict_rate (alert > 0.5%); sample ustore for duplicate first_seen entries per url_hash; track per-key QPS with hotness alert on any url_hash > 100 ops/sec; correlate duplicate frontier enqueues against ustore write logs.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why URL Storage lives in this crawler The problem demands avoiding URL-level duplicates across **billions of URLs** — and the Bloom filter sitting in front of useen is probabilistic, with a ~1% false-positive rate. That means 1% of the time the Bloom filter says "probably seen" about a URL that might actually be new. Without a durable source of truth to consult on those maybe-hits, the crawler would silently drop ~1% of genuinely-new URLs forever. URL Storage is that source of truth: a persistent record of every URL the crawler has ever considered, with enough metadata (first-seen timestamp, status, last-fetched) to support freshness re-crawls and operator debugging. It's also what makes crash recovery possible — when the 12 GB in-RAM Bloom filter evaporates on a node restart, ustore is what you replay from to rebuild it. ## What happens without it Strip ustore out and two things break. First, every Bloom false-positive becomes a silent lost URL — the crawler's recall quietly degrades and nobody notices because there's no ground truth to compare against. Second, on any Bloom filter crash or corruption, the crawler has total amnesia: it re-enqueues every URL it's ever seen, fetcher throughput collapses into redundant re-fetches, and content-seen downstream has to absorb the duplicate flood after paying for full fetches. ## The number At 1B pages/month crawled with a ~3× discovered:crawled ratio, ustore ingests **~3B new URL rows/month** (~1,160 PUTs/sec sustained). At 100 bytes/row that's 300 GB/month of growth — well beyond anything you'd keep in RAM alone, but trivially handled by a sharded RocksDB or Cassandra cluster. ## Trade-off The designer accepted 3–10ms DB lookups on the ~1% Bloom-hit path as the price for durability and crash recovery, rather than trusting the in-memory filter alone.

operations.title: Crawl one URL (happy path)
operations.name: Crawl one URL (happy path)
operations.description: URL is popped from the frontier, fetched, parsed, stored, and newly discovered links are enqueued.

steps.title: Worker picks a back queue that's off cool-down
steps.action: The frontier scheduler scans back queues and selects one whose host is out of its 500ms politeness window. It pops the head URL.
steps.codeOrCommand:
now = time.now
for bq in back_queues: if bq.next_earliest_fetch <= now: url = bq.pop bq.next_earliest_fetch = now + 500ms break

steps.title: Fetcher resolves host and issues HTTP GET
steps.action: A fetcher coroutine picks up the URL. First it checks its local robots.txt cache for example.com — a hit, and the path is allowed. It proceeds.
steps.codeOrCommand:
rules = robots_cache.get('example.com')
if not rules.allows('/p1', user_agent='MyCrawler/1.0'): return DROPPED
ip = dns.resolve('example.com')
resp = http.get('https://example.com/p1', headers={'User-Agent':'MyCrawler/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot)'}, timeout=(3, 15))

steps.title: DNS cache returns IP (hit)
steps.action: example.com is a popular host, so its A record is already cached locally in unbound. Sub-millisecond lookup.
steps.codeOrCommand:
unbound-control lookup example.com
# cached A 93.184.216.34, TTL 2h12m remaining

steps.title: Fetcher receives HTML body
steps.action: TLS handshake + GET returns 200 OK with 142 KB of HTML in ~380ms. The body is streamed into memory with a 10 MB cap.
steps.codeOrCommand:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 142384
Last-Modified: Tue, 21 Apr 2026 08:12:00 GMT <!DOCTYPE html><html>...

steps.title: Parser normalizes content and hashes it
steps.action: The parser extracts main text, normalizes whitespace/case, and computes SHA-256. It checks the content-seen store to see if we've already indexed this bytes-identical page under another URL.
steps.codeOrCommand:
text = readability.extract(html)
norm = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text.lower).strip
content_hash = hashlib.sha256(norm.encode).hexdigest
# 'a1b2c3...e4f5' (32 bytes)

steps.title: Content-seen says NEW
steps.action: The hash is not present. Parser marks the page as new content and writes the hash back so future mirrors are recognized.

steps.title: Parser persists page to WARC (parallel)
steps.action: HTML + metadata appended to today's open WARC file on S3. Done in parallel with link extraction — storage latency does not block the crawl.
steps.codeOrCommand:
warc_writer.append( url='https://example.com/p1', ip='93.184.216.34', fetch_ts='2026-04-24T10:15:42Z', content_hash='a1b2c3...e4f5', body=html_bytes
)

steps.title: Extractor pulls outbound links
steps.action: Walks the DOM, collects <a href>, resolves to absolute URLs, normalizes each. Discovered 47 unique outbound URLs on this page.
steps.codeOrCommand:
links = for a in dom.select('a[href]'): href = urljoin('https://example.com/p1', a['href']) href = normalize(href) # lowercase host, strip #frag, sort qs if href.startswith(('http://', 'https://')): links.append((href, depth+1))
# 47 unique links

steps.title: Filter applies robots + blocklist per URL
steps.action: For each of the 47 URLs, the filter consults the local robots cache, domain blocklist, and quota counters. 43 pass; 4 are dropped (2 robots-disallowed, 1 blocklisted adware host, 1 over-quota).
steps.codeOrCommand:
passed = for u, depth in links: if u.scheme not in ALLOWED_SCHEMES: continue if domain_blocklist.contains(host(u)): continue if not robots_cache[host(u)].allows(path(u)): continue if quota.over(host(u)): continue passed.append((u, depth))
# 43 of 47 passed

steps.title: URL-seen dedupe via Bloom filter
steps.action: Each URL is hashed and checked against the Bloom filter first. Of the 43, the Bloom filter says 30 are DEFINITELY new (Bloom miss — skip DB), 13 are MAYBE seen (Bloom hit — consult DB). DB confirms 12 truly seen, 1 was a Bloom false positive. Net: 31 new URLs get added to both tiers.
steps.codeOrCommand:
new = for u, depth in passed: h = hash64(u) if not bloom.mightContain(h): new.append((u, depth)) # definitely new — skip DB bloom.add(h) db.put(h, {'first_seen': now}) else: if db.get(h) is None: # Bloom false positive new.append((u, depth)) db.put(h, {'first_seen': now})
# 31 new URLs

steps.title: New URLs enqueued into appropriate back queues
steps.action: The router inspects each URL's host, assigns to a front queue by priority, and appends to the host's back queue. The crawl frontier grows by 31.
steps.codeOrCommand:
for u, depth in new: pri = priority_band(u) # 1..5 front_queues[pri].push(u, depth)
# router thread moves from front → back in background

operations.title: Duplicate content detected
operations.name: Duplicate content detected
operations.description: The URL is fetched successfully but its normalized content matches a hash we've already indexed — skip storage but still mine the page for outbound links.

steps.title: Pop next URL
steps.action: A mirror URL (https://mirror.example.net/p1) pops off the frontier.

steps.title: Fetch succeeds with identical bytes
steps.action: Mirror returns the same page as https://example.com/p1 (content-identical CDN copy).

steps.title: Parser hashes the normalized content
steps.action: Same normalization pipeline → same SHA-256. Check content-seen.

steps.title: Content-seen HIT — duplicate!
steps.action: The hash exists from 12 seconds ago. The parser now knows this page is a duplicate; it will NOT write to the page store, but will still extract links.
steps.decision: content hash already indexed — SKIP page store, still extract links

steps.title: Extract links anyway
steps.action: Even though content is a dup, the mirror may link to fresh URLs that the canonical didn't. Extract and normalize all hrefs.
steps.codeOrCommand: links = [normalize(urljoin(base, a['href'])) for a in dom.select('a[href]')]

steps.title: Filter
steps.action: Same filter pipeline as happy path.

steps.title: URL-seen dedupe
steps.action: These URLs have already been fed through when we crawled the canonical — Bloom + DB confirm ALL 43 are already seen. Zero new URLs.
steps.codeOrCommand:
new = for u,d in passed: if bloom.mightContain(hash64(u)): if db.get(hash64(u)): continue # truly seen new.append((u,d))
# 0 new
steps.decision: zero new URLs discovered via this mirror — net crawler progress = 0

operations.title: robots.txt disallows the path
operations.name: robots.txt disallows the path
operations.description: Worker is about to fetch a URL but the host's robots.txt disallows it. The URL is dropped politely before any HTTP request is made.

steps.title: Pop URL for strict-host.com
steps.action: A URL for strict-host.com (a site with a restrictive robots.txt) is dispatched.

steps.title: Fetcher checks robots.txt cache
steps.action: Fetcher looks up strict-host.com in its local robots cache. Cache miss (first contact today) → fetch /robots.txt itself first.
steps.codeOrCommand:
rules = robots_cache.get('strict-host.com')
if rules is None: r = http.get('https://strict-host.com/robots.txt', timeout=5) rules = RobotFileParser(r.text) robots_cache.put('strict-host.com', rules, ttl=24h)

steps.title: DNS resolves strict-host.com
steps.action: Fresh lookup (cache miss, new host today). Adds ~40ms on first contact.

steps.title: Filter evaluates robots rules against path
steps.action: robots.txt contains `User-agent: * / Disallow: /private/`. The target path matches. Filter rejects the URL.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# robots.txt fetched
User-agent: *
Disallow: /private/
Disallow: /admin/
Allow: / rules.allows('/private/report.pdf', 'MyCrawler/1.0')
# → False
steps.decision: robots.txt disallows /private/ — DROP URL, do not fetch
steps.note: A polite crawler never even makes the TCP connection to the disallowed resource. The URL is simply discarded; we don't retry later.

steps.title: Mark URL as seen anyway
steps.action: We still record the URL in the seen set so we don't re-evaluate it every time it's linked to. This also keeps a rejected-URL metric.

tradeoffs.decision: BFS traversal with per-host politeness vs DFS
tradeoffs.rationale: DFS concentrates traffic on one host and has unbounded depth on the web; BFS with back queues spreads load and bounds the damage any single misbehaving site can do.

tradeoffs.decision: URL-seen check on Bloom filter vs direct DB lookup
tradeoffs.chosen: Bloom filter in front of authoritative store
tradeoffs.rationale: A 12 GB Bloom filter serves 10^10 entries at 1% FPP with ~200 ns lookups; direct DB lookups would multiply read IOPS by the extraction rate and cost far more than the occasional re-crawl a false positive would imply.

tradeoffs.decision: Content dedup via exact hash vs shingle fingerprint
tradeoffs.chosen: Exact MD5/SHA-256 of the normalized body
tradeoffs.rationale: Exact hashing is cheap and catches the vast majority of true duplicates (mirrors, syndication). Shingle or SimHash would catch near-duplicates too but triples the hash DB size and slows the hot path; defer to a batch job if needed.

tradeoffs.decision: Trust robots.txt Crawl-Delay vs derive politeness from measured latency
tradeoffs.chosen: Trust Crawl-Delay with a floor of 500 ms, fall back to measured
tradeoffs.rationale: Respecting the site operator intent is the right default and avoids legal and reputational risk. The floor keeps us polite when sites omit Crawl-Delay or set it unrealistically low.

tradeoffs.decision: Frontier persistence (in-memory vs on-disk with snapshots)
tradeoffs.rationale: An in-memory frontier loses tens of millions of pending URLs on restart. A RocksDB-backed queue with snapshots every few minutes caps recovery to minutes at a small throughput cost.

interviewFollowUps.question: How would you keep the frontier balanced across hosts if one host dominates the outbound link graph?
How do you crawl JavaScript-rendered pages without blowing up per-page fetch cost?
How do you detect and handle crawler traps (infinite calendars, session-id parameter explosions)?
How would you re-crawl changed pages on a schedule without blowing the politeness budget?
How would you shard the URL-seen database across regions and still handle cross-shard extractor writes?
